title: The Afternoon Brief: Liverpool's new ownership, LIV's money crisis, and Mourinho returns
dek: A Bezos-led consortium takes 38% of Liverpool with a path to control, LIV Golf hemorrhages $30 million in prize money and faces vendor revolt, and José Mourinho is unveiled at Real Madrid after 13 years away.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Three sports institutions are in motion at once: Liverpool's ownership is in formal transition pending regulatory approval, LIV Golf is racing against a funding cliff with unpaid invoices piling up, and Real Madrid has installed a manager returning to the club for the first time since 2013.
bottom_line: Liverpool's new ownership is moving toward regulatory sign-off on Bhatia's vice-chairman role, with a 12-month option for controlling stakes that could reshape the club entirely. LIV Golf is executing emergency prize-money cuts while vendor invoices pile up unpaid and the league races to close BC Partners investment before the Saudi funding ends. Mourinho begins his Real Madrid tenure Saturday against Espanyol with six new signings integrated into the squad. Watch for: regulatory approval at Liverpool, any court filings from LIV vendors or announcements on BC Partners, Real Madrid's early integration of new players, and whether the Premier League's transparency on refereeing decisions shifts how clubs and fans view VAR's influence.
body: The morning's major story on ownership and capital has only deepened: a consortium named 1892 Holdings, led by British-Indian businessman Amit Bhatia and including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, has acquired approximately 38% of Liverpool FC from Fenway Sports Group under a definitive agreement, according to the desk's reporting. The deal values Liverpool between £5bn and £6bn. Bhatia will become vice-chairman pending regulatory approval and holds a 12-month option to acquire controlling interest, a mechanism that transforms what is now a minority stake into a potential fundamental ownership shift if exercised.

Meanwhile, the LIV Golf crisis has accelerated into a liquidity emergency. The league canceled its Michigan team championship and cut prize money at this week's Indianapolis finale, erasing $30 million in total payouts: the Indianapolis individual purse drops from $20 million to $10.1 million, with the winner's check falling from $4 million to $2.02 million. As the desk reported earlier, vendors report unpaid invoices ranging from thousands to nearly $100,000, with minimal response from the league's accounts receivable and legal departments. Mobii Systems Group, which supplied LIV's streaming technology, claims the league owes it more than $1.1 million for breach of contract and unpaid invoices. One unnamed contractor told the desk: "There's no response from the accounts receivable department. Even their legal counsel has not responded to demand letters." The withholding pattern, combined with 30-day termination notices to some contractors and the Saudi Public Investment Fund's halt to funding this month, has led restructuring experts to speculate that LIV may be preparing for bankruptcy. The league is actively seeking new investment from BC Partners, but the timing is acute: without new capital before vendor claims accelerate, the league faces formal restructuring.

On the field, José Mourinho was officially presented as Real Madrid manager on Tuesday after signing a three-year contract, returning to the club for the first time as head coach since 2013. Mourinho told Real Madrid TV his return carries emotional weight alongside professional standing: "Real Madrid, from a professional point of view, is the top of a coach's career. That's the professional side. Then, there's the emotional side. It's like coming home. Emotionally, it's more beautiful than the first time I came." Real Madrid have added six new signings and face Espanyol in their opening league game on Saturday.

Elsewhere, the Premier League will publish the full verdicts of its Key Match Incidents Panel on referee and video assistant referee decisions for the first time this season, ending a policy of private judgment. The panel comprises five members, three former players and coaches, one Premier League representative, and one from Pro Ref, and will have its rulings shared publicly via the league's platforms. The shift marks a move toward transparency on officiating, though Ifab's continued refusal to permit live VAR broadcast leaves gaps in full visibility.

In golf, Scottie Scheffler, ranked world number one, won the FedEx St. Jude Championship by eight shots at TPC Southwind, opening the FedEx Cup Playoffs with a commanding margin. In the AFL, the tribunal upheld Jacob van Rooyen's three-match suspension for a striking incident that knocked out Port Adelaide's Aliir Aliir, rejecting Melbourne's appeal and the club's submitted biomechanist evidence. Van Rooyen will miss Saturday's game against the Western Bulldogs and the Demons' first two finals matches.
